Issued at 323 PM EST Sun Nov 22 2026

===== Rain and Warmth End Tonight, Followed By Quite Coolness =====

Unseasonable warmth continues in the immediate short term awaiting 
the incoming rain and cold front to get here and cool us down for 
tomorrow. Until then, there will be a large band of rain moving in 
from the west. Ahead of the rain lies a decently dry air mass and 
lessening daytime heating. Rainfall totals should continue trending 
downwards as this moves east over our CWA, with highest totals west 
of I-65. SW flow will try to moisten the atmosphere, with PWATs 
reaching an 1.0", but will more so ensure that everyone sees at 
least some rain. According to the latest REFS guidance, southern IN 
counties have about a 25% chance or less of seeing more than 0.5", 
with most places seeing 0.25" or less as the rain moves eastwards.

Behind the rainfall, winds will increase and shift out of the NW. In 
fact, we could have overnight wind gusts near 15-25 MPH, lessening 
through Monday morning. This would be from the passage of a cold 
front overnight and a tightening pressure gradient as a high 
pressure builds in at the surface. This also means cooler air is on 
its way for Monday morning. Beginning tomorrow, there will be a 
decent temperature gradient oriented with coolest temps in Dubois 
County with the warmest morning lows in the Lake Cumberland as 
they'll take the longest to clear clouds and experience the cool NW 
flow. Thus, temperatures will range from the low 30s in the NW CWA, 
to mid or upper 40s in the far SE. 

Eventually, everyone gets behind the cold front for a dry and cool 
Monday afternoon. Skies will clear by the afternoon although highs 
only recover into the low to mid 50s. Lows Monday night will be cold 
in the mid 20s to low 30s. Once the surface ridge builds in, we then 
will have quiet weather until a new system forms along the Gulf 
associated with an impulse of energy of a shortwave from the 
southern Rockies/northern Texas area. So before I put the cart 
before the horse, Tuesday is quiet as well with highs in the upper 
40s and low 50s. Clouds will increase in the latter half of the day 
from the pair of shortwaves coming off the Rockies. With the surface 
high departing late Tuesday into Wednesday, this will set the stage 
for our next system to take shape. To end this short term 
discussion, lows Tuesday into Wednesday will be cold in the low to 
mid 30s.

===== Next System and Cold Rain by Midweek =====

Wednesday begins quiet with the increasing cloud cover. Starting out 
chilly in the 30s, southerly flow ahead of the next system will 
bring temperatures into the 40s and 50s by the afternoon. As clouds 
begin to thicken Wednesday morning, some light showers or sprinkles 
are possible across our southern communities. By Wednesday morning 
however, the pair of mid-upper level shortwaves will work in tandem 
and begin to strengthen a surface level low forming along the Gulf. 
The southernmost impulse of the pair will begin tapping into the 
Subtropical Jet for moisture. As this happens, the 2 PVU surface 
will lower in the atmosphere as well, providing more energy for the 
surface low to form. Being pulled north from phasing with the two 
mid-upper level impulses, the surface low will make a beeline 
straight for central KY, bringing a steady rain that may become 
heavy at times. Despite the phasing, a secondary low from deep 
within the Gulf will also phase and take over as the primary low 
along the southeast coast, with model solutions dropping the low 
down to 990 mb or less. What that means is that we'll have a pretty 
energetic system on our hands. 

Mentioned previously, the 2 PVU surface will lower allowing the 
primary surface low to strengthen. This will deepen the mid-upper 
level response and cool the atmosphere above our heads during the 
day on Wednesday and into Thursday. 1000-500 mb thickness will drop 
as a result with a continued, steady, moderate rainfall on Thursday. 
Temperatures will remain cool in the 40s on Thursday as the primary 
surface low begins to move towards the US Northeast heading into 
Friday morning. Should the strengthening low draw in enough cold air 
at mid-upper levels and should precip rates be heavy enough, there 
is a very small, non-zero chance that a rain/snow mix could develop 
over central KY overnight into Friday morning. There is too much 
uncertainty with this, but any impacts are expected to be minimal as 
temperatures at the surface may stay above freezing the entire 
event. Combined with warm surfaces and rainfall beforehand, a 
rain/snow mix would just be something to see and likely be missed if 
it happens overnight-early Friday morning. There's also the question
